clues: A 1928 wet market turned food centre, opposite a Buddhist temple with a tooth relic
The chicken rice queue here has its own tourist signage
Green-painted steel trusses, no air-con, packed at 12.30pm sharp
fact: Opened in 1928 as Maxwell Market. Tian Tian's queue got so famous the stall next door renamed itself to catch the overflow.

clues: 168 stalls under one roof — one of the largest in Singapore
Named after the runway that used to be next door
Lor mee, rojak and Hokkien mee stalls that all opened before 1980
fact: Built 1973 beside the old Kallang Airport. Locals still argue whether the lor mee or the Hokkien mee is the reason to queue.

clues: Over 200 cooked-food stalls — the biggest hawker centre in the country
You go up an escalator past a wet market to reach the food
A soya sauce chicken stall here got a Michelin star in 2016
fact: Largest hawker centre in Singapore. Hawker Chan's soya sauce chicken rice was the cheapest Michelin-starred meal in the world when it got its star.

clues: Sits inside an art-deco estate of curved white walkways and spiral staircases
Rebuilt in 2006, two storeys, wet market below
Chwee kueh and lor mee are the reasons people cross the island
fact: The surrounding estate is Singapore's oldest public housing, built in the 1930s. The market was rebuilt in 2006 but kept its stallholders.

clues: The bus terminal outside is the end of the line — literally
A ferry point to Pulau Ubin is a two-minute walk away
Famous for nasi lemak stalls that open until 3am
fact: The nasi lemak stalls here run past midnight because the crowd is half supper crowd, half people who missed the last ferry.

clues: Wet market, hawker centre and sari shops stacked in one building
Directly across the road from an MRT station on the North East and Downtown lines
Biryani, murtabak and Indian rojak within three stalls of each other
fact: The name comes from 'tek kia kha' — Hokkien for 'foot of the small bamboos'. Rebuilt in 1980 and again in 2009.

clues: A brutalist 1970s slab block on Beach Road, near the Thai supermarket strip
Known for a beef kway teow stall and a fried carrot cake stall on the same floor
Not the same building as the one everyone calls 'Little Thailand'
fact: Often confused with Golden Mile Complex next door. The food centre is a separate, older block.

clues: Opened 2017, sits inside a park, no walls on two sides
Run by a social enterprise operator, not NEA directly
Tray return here is actually enforced
fact: One of the 'new generation' hawker centres built after 2015, when the government restarted hawker centre construction after a 30-year pause.

clues: Sits under a block that also holds a polyclinic, a childcare centre and flats for seniors
Won a World Building of the Year award in 2018
Rooftop community farm above you
fact: The whole development won World Building of the Year 2018 — a hawker centre, medical centre, childcare and elderly housing stacked vertically.

clues: Tucked behind an old HDB estate between Buona Vista and Holland Village
The chwee kueh stall has a queue before 8am
Rebuilt around 2014, red-brick surroundings, low-rise blocks
fact: The estate around it dates to the late 1970s. The market was upgraded in 2014 and most original stallholders returned.

clues: Named after a brickworks that used to operate on the site
Off Jalan Bukit Merah, ringed by 1970s point blocks
The Hokkien mee and the char kway teow both have followings
fact: ABC stands for Alexandra Brickworks Company. The kilns are long gone; the name stuck.

clues: Two floors, wedged among shophouses and office towers in the CBD
Dies completely on weekends — it feeds the lunch crowd
A hand-made fishball noodle stall here sells out by 1pm
fact: Almost entirely a weekday operation. Many stalls simply don't open on Sundays because the offices around it are empty.

clues: Everyone calls it by a block number, not its official name
The bak chor mee queue starts after 8pm
Bedok North, and it's busiest close to midnight
fact: Officially Fengshan Market and Food Centre — but nobody calls it that. To the whole island it is 'Bedok 85'.

clues: The word 'Hainanese' is in its official name
Named for the village that stood here before the HDB blocks
Hougang, and the block number is in the name everyone uses
fact: Named after the Hainanese village that occupied this stretch of Hougang before redevelopment.

clues: Sits in a landed estate the British laid out in the 1950s
Surrounded by a shopping street locals call 'the circus'
No MRT within walking distance, which keeps the crowd local
fact: The estate was built in the 1950s for British servicemen. The roundabout beside it is still called Serangoon Garden Circus.

clues: Open-air, ringed by tall trees, right beside an MRT interchange
Appeared in a 2018 Hollywood film about a wedding
Satay and BBQ stingray stalls that will absolutely try to upsell you
fact: Featured in Crazy Rich Asians (2018). Local reaction was mixed — plenty of Singaporeans thought the film should have picked a less touristy centre.

clues: Small, roadside, beside a major expressway junction near the Botanic Gardens
Best known for nasi lemak and a long-running mee rebus stall
Mostly halal stalls, open late
fact: A small centre with an outsized reputation — the nasi lemak stall here has been running since the 1970s.

clues: Victorian cast-iron octagon, shipped in from Glasgow in 1894
A national monument that still sells food
The satay street outside only opens after 7pm, when the road closes
fact: The cast-iron structure was prefabricated in Glasgow and shipped to Singapore in 1894. Gazetted a national monument in 1973.

clues: Built to look like a Malay kampung village, timber-toned roofs
The wet market below is the busiest of its kind in Singapore
Goes completely mad during Ramadan
fact: Rebuilt in 2009 in a Malay village architectural style. The surrounding bazaar during Ramadan draws crowds from the whole island.

clues: Single-storey, low roof, beside a row of car workshops and a park connector
The Hainanese curry rice and the char siew stalls both draw queues
Nearest MRT is Redhill, but it's a real walk
fact: A low-rise 1970s centre that survived the estate's redevelopment around it.

item: One plate steamed chicken rice, no drink
clues: Famous stall
Central, tourist-heavy hawker centre
Cash and PayNow only
fact: Tourist-facing stalls in the CBD have drifted well above the heartland price for the same plate.

clues: CBD lunch crowd
No prices displayed on the tray rack
You did not ask before pointing
fact: The great national grievance: cai png stalls rarely display prices, and the same three dishes vary by more than $3 across the island.

clues: Heartland, not CBD
Uncle has run this stall for 30 years
Served in a glass, not a cup
fact: The kopi price is Singapore's unofficial inflation index — it moves maybe 10 cents a year, and everyone notices when it does.

item: Small plate char kway teow, with cockles
clues: Long-standing stall, 40-minute queue
East side
Cash only, uncle cooks one plate at a time
fact: Cockles are the swing factor — plenty of stalls now charge extra for them, or leave them out unless you ask.

clues: Little India
Served with fish curry, no extra charge
Open from 6am
fact: Plain prata is one of the last items still under $2 at most stalls — the egg prata is where the margin lives.

clues: Bukit Merah
Cooked over charcoal
Comes with sambal and a wedge of lime
fact: Charcoal-fired Hokkien mee stalls are getting rare — most have switched to gas, which regulars insist they can taste.

item: Nasi lemak with chicken wing and egg
clues: Far east, near the ferry terminal
Queue at 11pm
Wrapped in paper, not styrofoam
fact: The late-night crowd here is a mix of supper-seekers and people who missed the last ferry to Pulau Ubin.

item: Dry mee pok with handmade fishballs
clues: CBD, weekday-only stall
Sells out before 1pm
Fishballs made that morning
fact: Handmade fishball stalls charge a premium and sell out early — the CBD lunch hour does the rest.

clues: Street closes at 7pm for the stalls
CBD, heavily touristed
Minimum order is ten sticks
fact: Satay Street operates only in the evening, when Boon Tat Street closes to traffic and the grills come out.

clues: Geylang Serai
Pulled from a height, twice
Served hot in a glass
fact: 'Tarik' means pulled — the aeration is the whole point, and stalls that skip it get quietly abandoned by regulars.
